evals.prompt: I run marketing for Quaylight, an observability vendor. Our annual event QuaylightCon pulls 2,400 people. This year 38 of our 52 sessions are Quaylight product content - deep dives, roadmap, certification. Our Slack is genuinely warm, we call attendees 'the Quaylight family' and people fly in from 30 countries on their own dime. The exec team wants the new tagline to be 'the vendor-neutral observability community gathering' and wants that language on the site, the prospectus and the CFP. Can you write up our positioning around that?
evals.expected_output: A positioning brief that places QuaylightCon at the vendor-owned pole, refuses the vendor-neutral claim on the single-vendor program share, offers rebalance-or-drop as the only two remedies, and proposes honest vendor-pole framing instead.
expectations: Places QuaylightCon at the vendor-owned end of the governance spectrum, justified by ownership and where surplus money goes rather than by the event's tone
States the vendor-neutral claim is forfeit because single-vendor program content (38 of 52 sessions, roughly 73%) exceeds the threshold
Names the threshold explicitly as roughly 30-40% single-vendor program content
Offers exactly two remedies for the neutrality claim: rebalance the CFP so single-vendor content falls under the line, or drop the claim
Rejects the warm Slack, the 'family' language and the self-funded travel as evidence of community governance
States that warm or belonging language is available at every point on the governance spectrum and is deliberately borrowed by vendor events
Does not recommend 'vendor-neutral', 'community-run' or an equivalent neutrality claim in any tagline or prospectus line
Names what the vendor pole can honestly claim instead, such as practitioner or builder framing, scale and access to launches, or an executive carrying the edition's thesis
Produces a positioning statement in the shape 'For [best-fit attendee], [event] is the [event category] that [unique value theme]'
Does not deliver a finished tagline or hero copy before audience, alternatives and category are settled
Presents 2-3 candidate positionings with trade-offs and one recommendation rather than a single answer
Adds a recurring neutrality audit measuring single-vendor share of program content against the same threshold

evals.prompt: Northbound is a 300-person data-engineering conference I run in Manchester, third edition next spring. There are two other data conferences in the north of England - Pipeline North and DataHaus - and honestly we blur together. I sat my four co-organizers down last week and we listed out what we think attendees would do if they didn't come to us. Can you build me a differentiation angle against those two so I can start writing the sponsor deck?
evals.expected_output: A competitive-alternatives map across all five types, per segment, with the organizers' guesses rejected as a basis and interviews specified before any differentiation claim is written.
expectations: Maps alternatives across all five types: direct rivals, adjacent events repurposed for the same job, doing the job without any event, sending a delegate instead, and doing nothing at all
Names doing nothing as frequently the largest true competitor rather than a marginal case
Includes a concrete eventless alternative such as watching the talks on video afterwards or living in the topic's Slack or Discord community
Includes sending one delegate to report back to the team as its own distinct alternative type
Rejects the four organizers' own guesses as a basis for differentiation and requires real interview answers first
Specifies interviewing roughly 15-20 people
Specifies interviewing the happiest repeat attendees and sponsors rather than prospects
Keeps separate alternative lists per segment instead of one blended ranking across attendees and sponsors

States that the sponsor's primary alternative typically differs from an individual attendee's, for example a rival vendor summit or running their own private event versus doing nothing or watching videos
Classifies Pipeline North and DataHaus by ownership and money flow rather than by their tone or marketing language
Runs the do-nothing diagnostic when do-nothing dominates, mapping causes such as acute-trigger gap, risk perception and inertia to different positioning answers
Does not produce a finished differentiation claim or sponsor-deck copy before the alternatives research exists

evals.prompt: We're launching ThreadFest next May - first edition, targeting about 150 people, and it's basically me part time plus two friends who help on weekends. Zero sponsors so far. The topic is the overlap between developer experience and internal documentation, and genuinely nothing out there covers exactly that. My plan is to invent and own a whole new conference category, 'the docs-ops summit', because if we define the category we own it and nobody can catch us. That's our moat. How do we build the positioning around that?
evals.expected_output: A category-strategy recommendation that refuses the new category on this edition's resources, prices the education tax, and starts the event as a named subcategory with an evolution path.
expectations: Ranks the market-category menu on separate axes for effort, value and efficiency rather than one blended order
States that efficiency never selects the new category, because it is simultaneously highest effort and highest value
Names the subcategory of an existing category as the default rung
Refuses the new category here, citing the unmet promotion condition: no multi-edition runway, no existing sponsor relationships, no established brand

Names the education tax concretely, including slower ticket and sponsor cycles because nothing maps to a known budget line, copy that must explain the concept itself, marketing spend at multiples of a known category's, and multiple editions before awareness exists
States that a first edition already carries unproven-event risk and a new category compounds it with the attendee not knowing how to judge the event
Recommends starting as a subcategory and evolving toward the new category once traction exists
Proposes at least one concrete subcategory name following a naming pattern such as [topic] for [vertical], format-modified [topic] conference, or [audience]-first [topic] event
Explains that a subcategory inherits the parent category's existing sponsor budget lines and audience understanding
Deletes 'for anyone who cares about docs' or any everyone-audience framing rather than listing it as a weaker option
Asks about the publication deadline, one-off versus compounding mandate, and the effort ceiling before committing to a ranking
Does not accept the user's 'moat' framing for the new category unchallenged

evals.prompt: Foundry Days is our volunteer-run platform engineering conference, second edition, about 250 people, tickets at cost. There's a much bigger paid event called PlatformScale run by a consultancy - 900 pounds a ticket and every keynote is basically a sales pitch for their services. We want our marketing to say plainly that we are not PlatformScale, name them, let people draw the conclusion. Draft that line for us. Side note, when a sponsor asked my four co-organizers last month what the event is, we each gave a different answer, which was awkward.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to name the rival, an archetype contrast sentence, the alignment-rubric diagnosis of the four different answers, and the two cheap levers published together.
expectations: Refuses to name PlatformScale or any specific rival event in the anti-positioning line
Produces a contrast sentence that names an archetype instead of a competitor
Uses the shape 'There are many [archetype] events. This is not one of them.'
Gives both reasons an archetype contrast is required: it does not age out when the rival changes strategy, and it cannot be read as an attack inviting public rebuttal
Classifies PlatformScale by ownership and money flow rather than accepting 'sales pitch' tone as the classification
Identifies four organizers giving four different answers as a positioning-alignment finding in its own right, not a communications or training problem
Scores the current state against the 0-10 alignment rubric and places it in the band where organizers describe the event differently from each other
States that 7 or above is the pass threshold and treats anything below it as unfinished work to iterate on
Recommends publishing the contrast sentence together with a public rationale for the event's structural choice, as the default pair
States that the two cheap levers tie on effort because the real cost is the decision behind each, not the writing
Does not recommend a rename or rebrand as the fix

evals.prompt: Our conference has been JVM Summit Krakow for six years. Program is still about 85% JVM content - Spring, Kotlin, GraalVM, the usual. Registrations were flat this year, 620 against 640 last year. The board is convinced the name is holding us back and wants to rename to 'Krakow Polyglot' to signal we're modern and to open up sponsor categories beyond the JVM vendors. We've already commissioned a logo and bought the domain. Can you write the launch announcement for the new name?
evals.expected_output: A rebrand gate that fails, a refusal to draft the announcement, direction to fix program scope first, and the compliance exposure a rename carries spelled out.
expectations: Runs the rebrand gate before drafting anything, asking whether the audience or content scope has already moved beyond what the current name promises
Concludes the gate fails, because the program is still roughly 85% JVM content
States the rename is off the table, not postponed
Directs the team to settle program scope first: either broaden the program deliberately, or narrow back to what the existing name promises and keep it
States the order is substance first and name second, and that a rename promising change rather than recording one reads as churn
Declines to produce the rename launch announcement copy
Notes that a justified rename must map old scope to new scope explicitly in the announcement itself
Flags rebrand as the only positioning lever carrying compliance exposure, naming trademark and domain clearance plus renaming the event across signed sponsor agreements, venue contracts and listings
States a rename cannot be quietly walked back the way a published sentence can
Does not treat the flat registration figures (620 against 640) as evidence the name is the cause
Recommends a cheaper lever instead, such as the contrast sentence or a public rationale for the event's structure
Does not attach any figure or percentage to what the rename would do for registrations or sponsor categories

evals.prompt: BuildJam is our 36-hour student hackathon, 400 participants, fourth year. A fintech sponsor has committed 40,000 euros in prizes on the condition that the whole campaign is built around the pool - they want 'Europe's biggest student hackathon prize' as the headline everywhere. Our marketing lead already drafted the tagline and had the hero image designed last week. Build the positioning out from that so we can brief the design agency on Friday.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of prize-led positioning as a known failure mode, learn/build/share plus beginner inclusion as the lead, the drafted tagline treated as an output rather than an input, and 2-3 candidates with a recommendation.
expectations: Rejects prize-led positioning as the lead and names it as a known failure mode rather than a stylistic preference
Recommends leading instead with learning, building, sharing, and explicit beginner inclusion
States that leading with prize size cedes ground and attracts the wrong room
Notes the format can remain genuinely competitive underneath while the positioning does not lead with prizes
States that positioning must be settled before the tagline and hero copy, and that deciding messaging first is the most common ordering error
Refuses to treat the already-drafted tagline and hero image as fixed inputs the positioning must serve
Keeps the 40,000 euro prize pool available as a proof point or supporting detail rather than the positioning itself
Chooses a best-fit attendee segment narrower than 'students' and does not position for everyone
Produces a positioning statement in the 'For [best-fit attendee], [event] is the [event category] that [unique value theme]' shape
States explicitly that first-time or non-programmer participants are welcome as part of the positioning
Presents 2-3 candidate positionings with trade-offs and one recommendation rather than executing the sponsor's brief directly

evals.prompt: Relay is our single-track frontend conference, five editions in, 700 attendees, curated end to end by our founder Ana who writes a newsletter with about 40,000 subscribers and personally picks every single speaker. We have nine months to the next edition and the ambition is that Relay becomes the thing people plan their year around for the next decade. Our sponsor deck currently says 'a marquee keynote lifts early registrations by 30%'. Should we lean harder into booking big-name keynotes? Where should we put our effort beyond just writing a positioning line?
evals.expected_output: A lever-investment recommendation promoting lineup-as-brand on the compounding mandate and curator, with the 30% headliner claim refused and removed, and the single-track choice published as an identity claim.
expectations: Refuses to use the '30% lift in early registrations' headliner claim, identifying it as speaker-bureau or PR advocacy rather than verified data
Recommends removing that claim from the sponsor deck rather than restating or softening it
Promotes lineup-as-brand for Relay, citing the compounding multi-edition mandate and a curator whose taste is genuinely the product
States lineup-as-brand is the starved option under a pure efficiency ranking: top on value but second on effort
Names the effort lineup-as-brand costs as a season of curation and invitations
Ranks the positioning-lever menu on separate axes including effort, value, efficiency and compliance cost, rather than one blended order
States rebrand is the only lever carrying compliance cost, and that the other levers tie at no review triggered and no reversibility spent
Applies the lineup benchmark question: can attendees say why these specific speakers are together
Treats a shrug on that benchmark as the lever not yet working, not as an individual speaker-quality problem
Recommends publishing the single-track choice as an explicit public identity claim rather than leaving the event undeclared in the middle
Distinguishes booking individually famous keynotes from lineup-as-brand, which turns on the coherence of the set
Does not recommend a rebrand or rename

evals.prompt: Kestrel is a four-year-old SRE conference, 900 attendees, we run it as a small company. Two problems. First, sponsors keep describing us to their colleagues as 'a recruiting fair', which is not what we are. Second, our sponsor-close cycle is running five months when the comparable conferences we know close in about six weeks. Our head of marketing wants to reposition the event every year so it stays fresh, and she's asking me for the industry benchmark number that links positioning quality to ticket sales so we can track it on the dashboard. What's that benchmark and how do we fix the two problems?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to supply a benchmark that does not exist, the 0-10 alignment rubric offered instead, both symptoms read as misdescription-watch triggers firing a category re-run, and annual repositioning rejected.
expectations: States plainly that no industry number ties positioning quality to ticket or sponsor outcomes, and declines to supply one
Does not invent or cite any percentage, conversion rate or benchmark figure linking positioning to ticket or sponsor results
Offers the 0-10 alignment rubric with a pass threshold of 7 or above as the judged measure instead
Identifies both reported symptoms as misdescription-watch triggers: sponsors consistently describing the event wrongly to colleagues, and a sponsor cycle far longer than category peers'
Recommends re-running the market-category step at the next edition on the strength of those triggers
Rejects repositioning every edition, giving the reason that returning attendees and sponsors are the asset
States that messaging may be adjusted more often than positioning, which is committed across multiple editions
Requires deciding in advance which proxy triggers which revision and writing both down before publishing
Names at least two further triggers from the misdescription watch list, such as arrivals expecting things the event does not deliver, or CFP submissions assuming capabilities the event lacks
Treats 'recruiting fair' as evidence the sponsor-side best-fit segment or value theme is wrong, rather than as a copy problem
Does not recommend a rename or rebrand as the fix
